findings.summary: Circuit acknowledgement is recorded per Master generation but honoured per episode, so a successor Master is never told
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. The ack models what one Master generation knows, but the gate reads it as a fact about the episode. Conditions observed: (told null, acked null) tell at once; (told set, acked null) retell every CIRCUIT_RETELL_MS; (acked by generation N) silent for the rest of the episode, including when the live Master is generation N+1. `_tellMasterOfCircuit` returns on `episode.masterAckedAt` alone; `master_acked_generation` is written by `circuit.ack` and read by nothing (`_episodeRow` does not even expose it); the `bridge_config_circuit_fixed` trigger makes `master_acked_at` immutable, so a new generation's ack can only replay as `already-acked`. Consequence: an episode that outlives the Master that acknowledged it (the gateway itself relaunches the Master with backoff) leaves the new Master unpushed and `tc bridge status` printing `Acknowledged <time>` with no sign it was a predecessor's, which is the 'Master goes on releasing while the chat is closed' case the telling exists to end. Either gate the telling and the status wording on `masterAckedGeneration === the live generation` and let a later generation acknowledge (the trigger then guards the pair, not the timestamp alone), or record in ADR 0023 that one acknowledgement binds every later Master and drop the unread column.

findings.summary: routesMasterNotTold reads a once-set timestamp while the telling itself is per route state
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Two signals answer 'has the Master been told of this route' and they disagree: `_tellMaster` keys `_state.mastersTold` on `routeId:v<version>` (told again for each state a route reaches), while `operatorStatus` counts untold routes with `!r.masterWakeAt`, a column `routes.noteMasterTold` sets and nothing clears. A route told once as `awaiting-master` that later becomes `reply-held` after the listener has gone is untold of its held reply yet is not counted, so the operator reads `routesMasterNotTold: 0` in exactly the case docs/operator-bridge.md ('If the listener goes away afterwards...') offers the field for. Derive the count from the same per-state fact the telling uses: persist the version (or state) the Master was last told of and compare it with the route's current one, or clear `master_wake_at` when a route changes to a state that needs the Master again.

findings.summary: The per-caller rate limit is applied after the write it is meant to bound, and its table never drops a caller
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. `handle` calls `_admit` only after `PRINCIPALS.helper` has returned, and that proof has already run `bridgeStore.nonces.claim(nonce)` for every helper write except the claim; the 429 is then a `_refuseLogged` line. So a helper past 600 a minute still inserts one `bridge_nonces` row and one log line per request, which is what the RATE_LIMITS comment says the limit prevents ('cannot fill the store or the audit'), and the refused request's nonce is spent. Separately `_admitted` is keyed by token id and by `projectId:launchId` and a key is only ever rewritten by its own caller, so each launch that ever offered a candidate and each rotated token keeps an entry (an empty or stale array) for the life of the server; `_admit`'s `name` parameter is unused. Admit before the nonce is consumed (prove the token, admit, then claim the nonce), and drop a key when its filtered list is empty or sweep the map from the gateway's tick.

findings.summary: The helper's inbound path was not updated for the two new refusals: a 429 RATE_LIMITED discards the operator's message as unacceptable
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. lib/bridge-api.js now answers every helper route `429 RATE_LIMITED` (one shared 600-a-minute bucket per token across inbound, claim, parts, ack and failure) and `403 LOOPBACK_REQUIRED`. The consumer, lib/bridge-helper/inbound.js#handleOne, counts a failure transient only when `status === 0 || status >= 500`, and REFUSAL_TEXT has no entry for either code, so a rate-limited hand-over is not retried: the message is dropped, logged `inbound-refused`, and the operator is told in Discord `Not delivered: TangleClaw could not accept this message.` The outbound side is unaffected (refusalKind maps unknown codes to `down` and the item waits), which is why this is the inbound path only. I found no helper-side test or doc line for either code (the only RATE_LIMITED and LOOPBACK_REQUIRED assertions are server-side in test/api-bridge-gateway.test.js), so there is no evidence the consumer's behaviour under the new contract was looked at. Consequence: in exactly the case the limit exists for, a helper gone wrong on the outbound side spends the shared bucket and the operator's messages are thrown away with a notice that sends them to rephrase rather than wait. Why it broke: the limit was added at the producer and the consumer's status classification predates it. Remedy: treat 429 as transient in handleOne (bounded retry, then the UNREACHABLE text, which already says to send again later), give LOOPBACK_REQUIRED its own closed text or log code, and add a relay test for each.

findings.summary: Helper doc says the bot is online only while the bridge is operational; the code and the runbooks do not make that so
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. docs/operator-bridge-helper.md ("What it will and will not do") ends its online bullet with: "The runbooks enable the bridge before starting the helper and stop the helper when rolling back, so that the bot is online only while all three hold." That contradicts the sentence before it ("Online proves one thing: the helper's Gateway connection") and the code. (1) lib/bridge-helper/cli.js run() starts the Gateway and identifies as online without asking the bridge anything; a disabled bridge only makes the outbound claim fail (409, `claim-failed`, back-off) while the Gateway connection, and so the online presence, stays up. (2) deploy/com.tangleclaw.bridge-helper.plist is KeepAlive + RunAtLoad, so once installed the helper comes online at every login whether or not the server is running, the bridge is enabled or a Master exists. (3) The roll-back runbook disables the bridge in step 1 and stops the helper in step 2, so the bot is online with the bridge disabled in between, and indefinitely if the operator disables it outside the runbook. (4) Nothing in the runbooks orders or holds the 'verified Master' condition: `operator/enable` checks only the Master's Medusa setting (`masterListenerEnabled`, lib/bridge-api.js operatorSwitch), not a live verified Master, and a Master that exits later leaves the helper online. Consequence: an operator who reads this sentence takes a green dot as proof the bridge is operational, which is the inference the commit set out to stop. Delete the sentence (the three-condition statement before it and step 7 of the activation runbook already say what is true); do not reword it into another guarantee unless a test pins it.

findings.summary: Activation step 7 expects `gateway: ready` straight after start, but `status` reads a snapshot written once per outbound pass
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. docs/runbooks/activate-the-operator-bridge.md step 7 runs `install-launchd`, then `status`, and expects `gateway: ready`; the runbook's standing rule is that a step whose expected result does not appear means roll back. `status` (lib/bridge-helper/cli.js status()) does not ask the running helper: it prints the `gateway` field of status.json, which run() writes only after each outbound pass (cli.js writeSnapshot call in the loop). The first pass is one local HTTP claim and normally finishes before Discord's READY arrives (GET /gateway/bot, the WebSocket handshake, HELLO, IDENTIFY), so the first snapshot records `connecting`, or `status` prints `gateway: no snapshot yet`, and it is not rewritten until the next pass: `pollSeconds` later (15 s by default) and up to 5 minutes when the helper is backing off. The same staleness applies the other way: a dropped or fatal Gateway still reads `ready` until the next pass. This matters more now that docs/operator-bridge-helper.md names `bin/tc-bridge-helper status` as the proof of the Gateway `ready` condition. Consequence: an operator following step 7 promptly sees `connecting` and rolls a healthy activation back. Either write the snapshot when the Gateway's state changes (READY, RESUMED, close, fatal), or have step 7 say to run `status` again after one poll interval before judging it; a test for whichever is chosen should start the helper and read `status` before the second pass.

findings.summary: Activation step 7 expects `gateway: ready` straight after install, but `status` reads a snapshot written only at the end of each outbound pass
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Why it broke: `status` (lib/bridge-helper/cli.js, `status()`) prints the Gateway state from the snapshot file, and `run()` writes that file only after `outbound.pass()` returns, never when the Gateway changes state. Read from the code, not from a run: `gateway.start()` is followed at once by the first pass, a loopback claim that returns while the Gateway is still fetching its URL and identifying, so the first snapshot most likely says `connecting`; the next one is written a poll interval later (15 s by default, up to 5 minutes while passes are failing and the loop backs off). Before the first pass there is either `gateway: no snapshot yet` or the previous run's snapshot, because `status` does not compare the snapshot's `pid` with the lock's pid. docs/runbooks/activate-the-operator-bridge.md step 7 says to run `install-launchd`, then `status`, and expect `gateway: ready`, and the runbook's rule is that a missing expected result means roll back and tell the Architect. Consequence: whoever runs this Tier 3 activation can roll back a healthy helper because of a reading that is up to one poll interval old, and the same lag sits under docs/operator-bridge-helper.md's `Send them again once status shows the Gateway ready`. The bot showing online in Discord is the prompt signal and `status` is the late one, which the two documents do not say. Either write the snapshot when the Gateway state changes (and have `status` ignore a snapshot whose pid is not the running helper's), or state in step 7 and in the helper page that `status` reflects the last pass and to read it again after one poll interval before treating it as a failed step. Minor, same step: the line printed is `helper: running (pid N)`, not `helper: running`.

findings.summary: The panel's click handler is not tied to the panel that is mounted, so a token can be drawn after settings closes
findings.recommendation: Scope: class (bounded to `tcMountOperatorBridge` in public/operator-bridge-panel.js). The click listener closes over the `panel` and `draw` of the first mount and runs `draw()` after `await panel.act(...)` whatever happened meanwhile. Two members: (1) Create the helper token, confirm, and close settings before the answer arrives: `tcForgetOperatorBridge` clears the token and empties the container, then the pending `mint-token` sets `state.token` and `draw()` writes it into the hidden dialog, where it stays until settings is next opened. That is the state the file's header, docs/operator-bridge.md and CHANGELOG say cannot occur ("gone when ... settings closes"). The window is one request long. (2) A second mount on the same container skips binding (`data-bridge-bound`) but replaces `mounted`: clicks would keep driving the first controller while `forget()` clears the second. Not reachable today, because `openGlobalSettings` rebuilds the section element on every open; the test `Mounting again binds nothing twice` pins the skipped bind and not which controller a click reaches. One construction closes both: have the handler read `mounted.get(container)` at click time, and have `forget()` mark the controller so that a late answer neither stores a token nor redraws. Add a test that forgets while a mint is in flight.

The Master's close (lib/bridge-api.js, `withdraw: true`) also runs `outbound.withdrawForRoute`, which withdraws every `ready` or `blocked` item of the route; the new path does not. A status or failure notice for that route still `ready` (most likely after a circuit reset with `withdraw`, since nothing was handed to the helper while the circuit was open) is then claimed and posted for a route that is closed: `leases.claim` selects on item state alone. The operator can be told a message is waiting on the Project Master after its route was closed. Either call `outbound.withdrawForRoute(row.route_id, { at })` in the loop and assert it in the withdraw-on-reply test, or, if leaving those notices to post is intended, drop "exactly as a close would have done" from the comment. The sweep selects every released route with a withdrawn reply, not only those this write withdrew; with every withdrawal now followed by the sweep in the same transaction the two sets are the same, so no change is needed there.

findings.summary: A retired index is refused at every boot but dropped only inside the migration, so the previous build re-creating it locks the merged build out
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance (lib/bridge-schema.js RETIRED_SCHEMA_OBJECTS, added in 1278fe19), with the construction generalising to any later retirement. Why it breaks: the drop lives only in upgradeBridgeTables (run when schema_version < 54), while the refusal lives in bridgeSchemaProblems, which createBridgeSchema runs on every boot (lib/store.js:466). The build on main at the base commit also runs createBridgeSchema on every boot (fed2bd15 lib/store.js:1594), and its bridgeIndexDdl contains 'CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_bridge_routes_conversation'; it does not list that index in its own shape check, and the code and docs state that an earlier server accepts a later store ('each later shape is a superset of the earlier ones', docs/operator-bridge.md lines 613 and 622). Read together: one boot of the previous build against a v54 store puts the index back, schema_version stays 54, and the merged build then throws 'index idx_bridge_routes_conversation was retired in v54 and is still present' at startup with no migration left to drop it. Who does what wrong: whoever returns to the previous build without restoring the store (rollback step 5 restores a whole-install backup, which loses everything written since, so skipping the restore is the tempting path; a developer switching a checkout between main and this branch hits the same) cannot start the merged build again until they run DROP INDEX by hand. This was derived by reading both ends, not by running them. Simpler construction: retire idempotently where the shape is created - have createBridgeSchema drop every RETIRED_SCHEMA_OBJECTS entry with retiredAt <= the current version before the shape check (DROP INDEX IF EXISTS is a no-op on a correct store), and keep the check as the proof that the drop held. If refusal is the intended behaviour, say so in the rollback runbook's step 5 and in the v54 paragraph of docs/operator-bridge.md, which today describes v54 only as additions and does not mention the retirement.

findings.summary: cross-component-contract: the gateway's own Medusa exchange is never closed, so main's watchdog (#2086) now raises it to the operator rung and it stays there
findings.recommendation: Scope: class (every exchange the gateway initiates; one send site, lib/bridge-gateway.js dispatch()). Why it broke: the exchange record waits for its initiator to close a reply-required exchange, and the gateway is an initiator that never closes and is not allowed to. Evidence, all read from HEAD: dispatch() sends through medusaSend.sendTracked with sessionId 'operator-bridge', senderProjectId null, caller {kind:'system'}, replyRequired true, so the row is tracked (the target is a local participant), normal priority, reply_required, sender_project_id NULL. 'replied' is not in medusa-exchanges TERMINAL_FACTS; _closeIfSatisfied skips reply_required rows; exchanges.close() admits only the operator or a verified launch of sender_project_id, which is NULL here; markRecipientRetired deliberately leaves a replied exchange 'for their initiator to close'. No bridge file calls close or any terminal transition (grep of lib/bridge-*.js for exchanges()/medusaExchanges shows only getByRequestId, getByHubId and bindHubId). Consequences now that main's watchdog runs beside it: (1) store.medusaExchanges.listOpen() gains one permanent row per answered route, and the watchdog reads each row's facts on every 30 s pass for ever. (2) #2086 gave normal mail an operator rung: _normalOperatorReason returns prolonged-unread / prolonged-actionable / prolonged-unanswered at operatorNormalMs (60 min), or configuration-hold at the aged rung. A bridge route whose target has not replied in that time, or whose route the Master has since closed, rerouted or let expire while the old exchange stays open, gets operator_alerted. bridge-notify._operatorNeeded reads that fact and posts 'A message to <project> has gone unanswered long enough to need you' to Discord, about the bridge's own message. (3) listEscalated() filters on terminal_at IS NULL and esc_level != 'none' only, so an exchange answered after it aged stays in GET /api/medusa/escalations, and one that reached the operator rung stays in escalationSummary's dashboard banner, until the operator closes it by hand. (4) The aged notice to the sender resolves to no workspace (_senderWorkspace: no sender project, and the gateway's workspace is not a localParticipant), so each one records escalation_undeliverable and logs a warning. Before the merge only (1), (4) and a permanent 'aged' row existed on the stack; (2) and the banner in (3) are new at this head. Remedy by construction rather than per site: give the exchange record a system-initiator close (a caller kind the gateway can prove, recorded as such) and have the gateway end its exchange wherever the route stops waiting on it: reply held, route closed, rerouted, expired, returned to Master. Then decide and record whether a still-routed, unanswered bridge exchange should reach the operator rung at all; if it should, that is a decision ADR 0023 P2 does not yet state. Add a test that drives a routed exchange past operatorNormalMs through the real watchdog tick and asserts what the operator is and is not told, and one that asserts no open tracked exchange remains after a route closes. I did not run anything; the timing claims are read from medusa-watchdog DEFAULTS and the code paths named.

findings.summary: A bridge route's own Medusa message can now reach the watchdog's operator rung, which the bridge doc says never happens and which raises a second Discord notice for the route
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Why it broke: the stack wrote its escalation claim against a watchdog in which normal-priority mail stopped at the sender, and main's #2086 (merged underneath it here) gave normal mail an operator rung. Established by reading, not by a run. (1) docs/operator-bridge.md, 'The one status notice', says 'The Medusa message itself is normal priority, so the delivery watchdog never raises it to its escalation or operator rungs.' The gateway does send a tracked, reply-required, normal-priority exchange (lib/bridge-gateway.js dispatch via sendTracked; test/bridge-gateway.test.js asserts priority 'normal'). In the merged tree lib/medusa-watchdog.js#_considerEscalation ages normal mail at agedNormalMs and then calls _alertOperator for any reason _normalOperatorReason names: configuration-hold at 30 minutes, prolonged-unread / prolonged-actionable / prolonged-unanswered at operatorNormalMs (60 minutes by default). tick() walks store.medusaExchanges.listOpen() with no exclusion for a system sender, so the bridge's exchange qualifies. Only the 'escalation' half of the doc sentence is still true. (2) The consequence is in code, not only prose: lib/bridge-notify.js#_operatorNeeded selects every 'operator_alerted' fact since the bridge was enabled, with no filter on who sent the exchange, so a route whose target does not answer for an hour gets its one 'status' item at 5 minutes and then an 'operator-needed' notification ('A message to <project> has gone unanswered long enough to need you.') in the helper's mailbox. ADR 0023 Decision 17 says of a route: at most one pending notice to Discord, 'It never climbs to the blocking, critical or operator-authority rungs', 'Nothing repeats', and that this is 'policy local to a route'. Who does what wrong: an operator or Master reading the doc or the ADR expects one notice per waiting route and gets two, and a maintainer tuning operatorNormalMs has no way to know it now sets when the bridge re-notifies Discord about its own routes. findings.summary: The bridge gateway never ends the reply-required exchanges it opens, so main's #2086 watchdog keeps judging and reporting them after the bridge is done with them
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance (one initiator, lib/bridge-gateway.js#dispatch). Why: dispatch sends through medusaSend.sendTracked with replyRequired: true and sender project null, and nothing in lib/bridge-*.js ever calls exchanges.close or retract (the only exchange calls are getByRequestId, getByHubId and bindHubId). A reply is not a terminal fact (TERMINAL_FACTS in lib/medusa-exchanges.js), and close() admits only the operator or a verified launch of the sending project, so the gateway's rows stay in store.medusaExchanges.listOpen until the target session is torn down. Consequences, each read from the code: (1) every answered bridge message stays in the watchdog's per-tick pass and in the #2086 tick meter for the life of the target session; (2) one that aged before it was answered stays in listEscalated, and one that reached the operator rung keeps the dashboard banner (escalationSummary) up with nobody able to clear it except the operator by hand; (3) a route the Master rerouted or closed leaves its earlier exchange open and unanswered, so about 60 minutes later the watchdog raises operator_alerted for it, which writes an activity row and, through lib/bridge-notify.js#_operatorNeeded, posts 'A message to <project> has gone unanswered long enough to need you' to Discord about a message the bridge already gave up on; (4) the aged notice and the recipient-retired notice have no sender workspace to go to (medusa-wake.localParticipant does not know the gateway), so each logs 'Medusa escalation notice undeliverable: no live session' at warn, including for exchanges that were answered. Remedy: have the gateway end its own exchange when the route stops waiting on that message (reply held, superseded by a reroute, route closed), through a system-capable close in lib/medusa-exchanges.js, and add a test that an answered and a superseded bridge exchange are no longer in listOpen.

findings.summary: The restore block copies the snapshot over the store without checking that the store is at rest
findings.recommendation: Scope: class, bounded to the lines between `launchctl bootout` and `cp` in the fenced block of docs/runbooks/roll-back-the-operator-bridge.md step 8 (lines 91-93). It broke because making the restore one fail-stop block removed the pause in which a person could inspect the store, while the two conditions that make the copy unsafe are still left to that person. Two members. (1) Line 91, `launchctl bootout ... || echo "the server was not loaded: going on"`, treats every bootout failure as 'not loaded'. A bootout that fails while the job is still loaded (or one aimed at a mistyped label) prints that reassurance and goes on to `git checkout` and `cp` under a running server that holds the store open. Nothing pins the target either: the test's launchctl stub records only `$1` (test/operator-bridge-runbooks.test.js line 178), so the label `com.tangleclaw.server` on the bootout line is compared with nothing, and changing it leaves the test green. (2) The store runs in SQLite's default rollback-journal mode (lib/store.js sets no journal_mode), and the server has KeepAlive, so in the one case this step is for (the v5.31.0 server failing at start, i.e. during migration) bootout can kill it mid-transaction and leave `tangleclaw.db-journal`. The block then copies the snapshot beside that journal, and the previous build replays it into the restored file on first open. The UNVERIFIED note (lines 107-110) asks the reader to move a journal aside 'before the copy', but the journal this creates appears between bootout and cp, inside a block pasted whole, so the instruction cannot be followed for it. Consequence: the release executor, on the last-resort path, gets a `restored:` line and a damaged store. What a fix takes: in the block, after bootout and before checkout/cp, (a) confirm the job is really gone (for example stop if `launchctl print "gui/$(id -u)/com.tangleclaw.server"` still succeeds) instead of inferring it from bootout's exit status, and (b) stop, or move it aside, when `"$STORE-journal"` exists. In the test, have the launchctl stub record its full arguments and assert the bootout target equals the Label in deploy/com.tangleclaw.server.plist, and add the still-loaded and journal-present cases to the block's run-as-printed test.

The `||` swallows every non-zero exit, not only the not-loaded one, and test/operator-bridge-runbooks.test.js lines 224-227 pin exactly that (a launchctl stub that fails bootout for no stated reason, and the block still runs checkout, cp and bootstrap). deploy/com.tangleclaw.server.plist sets KeepAlive true, and step 8 is for a server that will not start, so the job is being restarted by launchd while the block runs. If bootout fails for any other reason (the job is still shutting down, the gui domain cannot be reached from this terminal), the block prints a sentence that is false, checks out the old commit and copies the snapshot over a store that a restarting server process may open at any moment, and only then stops at `launchctl bootstrap` because the job is still loaded. The operator is left with no `restored:` line and no branch in the step that says what state that is: lines 99-103 cover a stop before bootout and a stop at `checkout` only, so a stop at `cp` (server stopped, old build checked out, store partly written) or at `bootstrap` (everything put back, server not started) has nothing to read it against. CHANGELOG.md line 85 also says the block 'stops at the first thing that fails', which is not so for this line. A fix takes: after bootout, confirm the job is really gone before going on (for example `launchctl print "gui/$(id -u)/com.tangleclaw.server"` must fail, otherwise exit with a message naming the job as still loaded), so that only the proven not-loaded case continues; add one result line each for a stop at `cp` and a stop at `bootstrap` saying what has and has not changed; and extend the stubbed test so that a bootout that fails while the job stays loaded stops the block before `checkout`.

findings.summary: Two things the restore depends on are prose after the block the operator is told to paste as it is
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Rollback step 8 says 'paste this as it is' (line 79) and then, below the block and its results, in the UNVERIFIED note at lines 107-110, asks for two things to be done before it: check the snapshot's sha256 against the receipt, and move a `tangleclaw.db-journal` aside before the copy. The block does neither. lib/store.js sets no journal mode, so the store uses SQLite's rollback journal, and a journal left beside the store is exactly what a server killed in the middle of a write leaves; step 8 kills a KeepAlive server that is failing at start-up, which is when the migration writes. If the journal is still there when `cp "$TC_SNAPSHOT" "$STORE"` runs, the block finishes, prints `restored:`, and the previous build then opens the snapshot and SQLite plays the old journal's pages into it. Nothing in the step's Expected lines would show that: the schema query reads one table. Likewise a snapshot changed or truncated since step 1 passes the block's only test of it, `[ -s ]`. So the one path in either runbook that replaces the live store can end in a damaged store with every success signal present. A fix takes putting both into the block where they stop it: after bootout and before `cp`, refuse (or move aside under a dated name, and say so) when `"$STORE-journal"` exists; and take the receipt's `sha256:` line as a fourth required variable and compare it with `shasum -a 256 "$TC_SNAPSHOT"` before the server is stopped. Then the note can lose both instructions, and the stubbed test at test/operator-bridge-runbooks.test.js lines 162-234 gains a case for each.

The 7 warning + 6 note finding(s) gate NOTHING: no gate reads them, so nothing in THIS review requires another round. (Whether the PR gate is satisfied, and whether the work cycle still owes a final/cumulative, are separate questions about coverage — ask them by running the gate, not by reviewing again.) Disposition each finding instead of reflexively fixing it — accept is the default for anything nobody will realistically action: `prawduct-hook disposition rev-20261004T224829Z-0c9f8851 <fid|oid> --accept "<reason>"`, which needs no review and moves no tree. If this branch has more judgeable work coming, there is a third route: carry the fix into the NEXT chunk's commit. That is NOT the deferral warned against above — deferring to a later ROUND buys a second round; riding a commit that is being made anyway buys none. Write it where that chunk will meet it (the build plan or `.prawduct/.handoff-notes.md`), or it is not a deferral, it is a drop. findings.summary: The snapshot block was not held to the rule the restore block was rewritten to: it can print an empty receipt line and still succeed
findings.recommendation: Scope: class, bounded to the two fenced blocks. The ruling's reason for the restore block is "a pipeline hides a failure from set -e" (tabletop finding 14). The snapshot block in activation step 1, which produces the five receipt lines the restore later requires, still ends with `echo "sha256:   $(shasum -a 256 "$SNAP" | cut -d' ' -f1)"`, and prints `commit:` and `schema:` from command substitutions inside an echo's arguments. Neither a failing pipeline member nor a failing substitution inside an argument stops a `set -e` block, so a failure there prints a labelled empty line and exits 0, and the step's Expected ("five lines") is still met. The receipt is the only source for TC_COMMIT, TC_SNAPSHOT_SHA256 and TC_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA, and the restore refuses an empty one, so the cost appears at the emergency, when nothing can supply the value. The likelihood is low (git and shasum have already run once on the same inputs); the point is that two blocks which were written as a pair now follow different rules, and the test's rule (`!/#|\|\s*(cut|awk|sed|head)\b/`) is applied to the restore alone and names tools rather than the construction. Assign each value to a variable first, as the restore does (`SUM=$(shasum …)`, `${SUM%% *}`), refuse an empty one, then echo; and apply one no-pipeline, no-comment assertion to every fenced sh block in both runbooks, written as "no single | outside ||" rather than a list of commands. The snapshot's integrity check could take `-readonly` at the same time, for the reason tabletop finding 11 gives.

Why it broke: 69a570ae added negated bracket patterns to blocks that the runbooks tell a person to paste into a terminal, and every proof of those blocks ran them non-interactively. Sites (all new since 829b0b7b): docs/runbooks/activate-the-operator-bridge.md lines 70 (`*[!0-9]*`), 74 (`*[!0-9a-f]*`), 129 (`*[!a-z_]*`); docs/runbooks/put-back-the-build-before-the-operator-bridge.md lines 62, 64, 66, 68 and their copies at 175, 177, 179, 181 (`*[!0-9a-f]*`, `*[!0-9]*`, `com.tangleclaw.*[!A-Za-z0-9.-]*`). The steps say 'in a terminal ... paste this as it is'; the default macOS terminal shell is an interactive zsh, where BANG_HIST is on and `!` followed by anything other than a blank, `=` or `(` starts a history reference, inside double quotes and inside `[...]` alike (bash exempts `[!`, zsh does not). I could not execute anything under this review's boundary, so confirm first: type `echo [!0-9]` at an interactive zsh prompt. Also correct the put-back runbook's closing note and the CHANGELOG line, which say the blocks were rehearsed 'under sh and zsh' without saying it was non-interactive.

findings.summary: The rule that an item never leaves a live lease is kept by each caller remembering to check, and two of this change's six fixes were callers that had not
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. lib/bridge-store.js states the invariant in `outbound.live`'s JSDoc ('An item never changes state under a live lease: nothing lets go of, withdraws, sets aside or delivers an item without settling the lease first'). Three signals have to agree for it to hold: the item's state (`ready`, `blocked`, `delivered`, `dropped`), its lease's state (`live`, `used`, lapsed) and its route's state (`released`, `closed`). Nothing owns that agreement. It is restated, in three different forms, at: `closeRoute` in lib/bridge-api.js (lapse, then `outbound.inFlight`); `applyRouteWrite` for any `decision.withdraw` (the same two calls, added here, which makes the bridge-api copy redundant); `applyOutboundWrite` (a direct lease SELECT, then the new cascade check); `applyCircuitReset` for `--withdraw` only (new); the retention sweep (a `NOT EXISTS` live-lease clause in SQL); and `markDelivered` (the new row proof, which exists because the item could have moved). `_withdraw`, which its own comment calls 'the one statement every withdrawal goes through', carries no lease predicate, and its call at the end of `applyCircuitReset` (`idem_key = ? AND state = 'ready'`, the circuit notice) runs for both decisions with no in-flight check at all. I could not show that a live lease on the circuit notice is reachable, so this is a warning, not a blocking finding. Consequence: the next write that withdraws or sets aside an item has to know to add the check, and fixes I and J in this bundle are two that did not. A construction closes the class; a seventh call site does not. Either put the predicate in `_withdraw` itself (`AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bridge_outbound_leases l WHERE l.outbound_id = bridge_outbound.outbound_id AND l.state = 'live')`, with callers comparing `changes` to what they expected), or add a `BEFORE UPDATE OF state ON bridge_outbound` trigger beside the existing lease triggers in lib/bridge-schema.js that aborts while a live lease exists. To find members, search bridge-store.js for `UPDATE bridge_outbound SET state`; expect the set-aside path (`state = 'blocked'`) as well as the withdrawals.

findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. The record of who was told (`_state.mastersTold`) is in memory, while master_wake_at is stored but not read by `_tellMaster`, so after a restart the first pass tells the Master again for each open route. That predates this commit, but every inbound now waits, so a restart re-sends one notice per waiting message rather than only for the unresolved few. Separately, a message for the Master produces two notices both worded "is waiting for you": one when it awaits routing and one immediately after the Master's own `--to master`. The commit message and docs/operator-bridge.md state this second one as intended. Neither strands or misroutes anything. If the repeat after restart matters, compare master_wake_at with updated_at before sending, as `routesMasterNotTold` already does.

findings.summary: A suggestion that cannot be computed leaves the route in accepted, where the Master cannot route it
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. In lib/bridge-gateway.js `_advance`, `suggestDestination` runs before the `suggest` step with no guard. If it throws (it reads aliases, projects, pins and earlier routes), the route stays `accepted` with no destination; `_needsMaster` is false for that state, so the Master is not summoned, and `tc bridge route` refuses it as `not-awaiting-master`. The inbound is not lost and the failure is visible: the route is already stored, every 15-second pass retries and logs `Bridge pass failed for a route` with the route id, and the operator still gets the five-minute waiting notice. So this is not an undetectable failure. The gap is only that advice which decides nothing can hold up the hand-off it accompanies. The readers involved are synchronous reads of the same database the step then writes, so a failure here most likely fails the step too and a guard would buy little; rated a note for that reason. If it is wanted, catching the failure and handing the route over with no suggestion and a reason code (failure_code allows any string up to 40 characters) would do it.

findings.summary: A Master outage cancels the open question: the gateway's 'queue' step ends it, and the operator's correlated reply is then refused
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. lib/bridge-store.js:2138-2148 ends the open question on any applied write whose resulting state is not exactly 'awaiting-master'. lib/bridge-gateway.js#_summonMaster (the `_step('queue', ...)` call, about line 827) moves an awaiting-master route to 'queued-master-unavailable' through that same applyRouteWrite whenever the Master is not live on a pass, so a held message with an open question has the question marked 'cancelled' the first time the Master cannot be had. After 'unqueue' the route is awaiting-master again with no open question; the operator's reply to the posted question gets 409 QUESTION_SETTLED, and the pending notice stays suppressed because questions.listFor is non-empty. This contradicts docs/operator-bridge.md ('Routing or closing the message without --answered-by ends an open question') and the design (a question ends by adoption, decline, cancel or expiry; the original stays held), and adoptVerdict itself treats 'queued-master-unavailable' as still held for the reply. No test covers a queue/unqueue with a question open. Fix: treat both Master-waiting states as held in that block (cancel only when the route leaves ['awaiting-master','queued-master-unavailable']), and add a test: ask, post, Master unavailable for a tick, Master back, reply adopted.

findings.summary: An open question and its route's state are kept in step at one of the sites that move a route, and that site reads 'queued because the Master is away' as 'no longer waiting'
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. Why it broke: 'this message is still held for the Master' is decided separately in three places that disagree, and the question's standing is derived from one of them. Conditions observed for one held message: (1) route awaiting-master, no question; (2) awaiting-master, question open, item unposted; (3) awaiting-master, question open, item posted; (4) question expired, route still held; (5) question adopted, route routed, reply route closed; (6) question cancelled, route routed or closed; (7) route queued-master-unavailable. The intended invariant is 'a question is open only while its route waits for the Master'. Two reachable breaks. (a) lib/bridge-store.js:2138-2148 cancels the open question on any applied write whose resulting state is not exactly 'awaiting-master'. The gateway's own 'queue' step (lib/bridge-gateway.js:828-831, through _step -> applyRouteWrite) sets 'queued-master-unavailable' whenever the Master is not live on a pass, so a Master that is away for one tick silently cancels every open question; 'unqueue' (gateway :834-835) returns the route to awaiting-master with the question cancelled, nobody is told, and the operator's reply to the question still visible in the chat is then refused 409 QUESTION_SETTLED. The same file treats that state as held in adoptVerdict (:1902) and settleOnReply (:1928), and _needsMaster (gateway :508) treats it as waiting on the Master; the comment at :2140 ('no longer waiting on the Master') is not true of it. Nothing in the plan's bounded design or the docs says a Master outage ends a question (docs/operator-bridge.md names only routing or closing without --answered-by), and no test covers it. (b) questions.settleOnReply closes the reply's route with its own UPDATE (lib/bridge-store.js:1926-1929), outside the check in (a). The reply route is an ordinary awaiting-master route the Master may itself have asked about; adopting it leaves that question 'open' on a closed route. At 24 hours expire() (:1323-1341) then bumps the closed route's version and queues the fixed sentence 'Your message is still held, and nothing has been sent on' for a message that was closed. Remedy by construction, not by a longer list: one owner that every route state change passes through decides what becomes of the route's open question from one definition of 'held for the Master' (the one adoptVerdict already uses), and settleOnReply's close goes through it. Decide and record whether a question outlives a Master outage; if it is meant to die there, say so in the docs and the Master's instructions and tell the operator. Tests: an open question across queue/unqueue; a question asked about a reply route that is then adopted. Search for other members: every 'UPDATE bridge_routes SET state' in lib/bridge-store.js (three sites today).

AND state IN ('ready','blocked')), decide what a live lease on it means for the route write (refuse outbound-in-flight, as close does, or let it post), and add the unposted-then-routed case to that test.

findings.summary: The pre-launch checks are not made immediately before the launch: an awaited warm-up of several seconds sits between them and launchSession
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Departs from the Architect's binding ruling 3 on the bounded design ("HELD and STOPPED both refuse bridge launch; every pre-launch condition is rechecked immediately before action") and from design section 2 step 7 ("is there a live session is asked immediately before, in the same synchronous step"), with no recorded decision. Why it broke: the launch seam bundles the asynchronous warm-up with the synchronous launch. Evidence: lib/bridge-gateway.js:903 runs _launchRefusal (project gone, archived, opted out, HELD/STOPPED, wrap running) and :908 reads store.sessions.getActive; :917 then awaits _deps.launchProject, whose first act (:116) is `await warmForLaunch(project)` (lib/launch-warmup.js: a CI probe of up to four sequential execs at 5 s each, lib/ci-status.js:47,145-171, alongside a 5 s checkout probe) before sessions.launchSession is called. The comment at :905-907 says the live-session question is asked "in the same synchronous step as the decision it guards"; it is not. What I verified it does NOT break: no second session is started, because launchSession is synchronous and refuses a second live session itself (lib/sessions.js:296-338), and no message is delivered on a held lane, because _awaitLaunch re-runs _launchRefusal. What it does break, during that window: (1) a HOLD placed on the lane is not honoured for the launch, since launchSession refuses only STOPPED, so a session is started on a held lane; the same holds for an opt-out, a wrap that starts, or the bridge being disabled (tick reads isEnabled only at its top, before several awaits). (2) A session started by hand in the window makes launchSession answer `Session already active` with no code, so the launch ends `launch-refused:REFUSED` and the operator is told it failed, where the design and docs/operator-bridge.md step 5 say that session is taken as the one to wait for. (3) tick has no re-entrancy guard and runs on a 15 s setInterval (server.js:4807, 12305); while a pass is suspended in the warm-up the launch row is still `queued`, so a second pass that starts meanwhile enters _beginLaunch for the same row, both reach launchSession, and the loser's refusal calls _launchFailed, whose launches.end (lib/bridge-store.js:2144, `WHERE settled_at IS NULL`) ends the row the winner has just moved to waiting-ready: a launch that succeeded is recorded failed and the message is never sent on. That needs a warm-up longer than the tick interval, which the four 5 s timeouts allow but a healthy host will not produce. Fix by construction: await the warm-up first, then do the route-held check, bridge-enabled check, _launchRefusal, the getActive question, the launchSession call and launches.begin with no await between them (split the seam into an async warm and a synchronous launch). The existing tests cannot see this because the stand-in for launchProject resolves at once; add a test whose stand-in changes the lane, and one that starts a session, while the warm-up is pending.

findings.summary: After a consented launch has been dispatched, the message can never again be routed to that project under any other session

Why it broke: the dispatch-time identity check is keyed on the route's newest launch row being `dispatched`, a state that is final, and not on this dispatch being the launch's own. Evidence: lib/bridge-gateway.js:603-607 returns the route to the Master with `identity-changed` whenever launches.latestFor(routeId) is `dispatched` for the destination project and the live target differs from the launch's session; the `bridge_launches_fixed` trigger makes that row permanent, and ask-launch cannot supersede it because it is refused TARGET_LIVE while the project runs (lib/bridge-api.js:651). So once the launched session has ended (it crashed before replying and the exchange failed, or it was replaced in the instant before the send, the case the test at 'READY that never comes...' ends on with "the Master decides again") and the project is running again under a new session, every later `tc bridge route` to that project by the Master's own decision is accepted and then bounced with `identity-changed`, and the operator is told each time that it "could not be sent to the session that was launched for it". Consequence: the Master cannot deliver the held message to the project it was meant for; it can only answer it itself or close it. It fails closed, so nothing is delivered to a wrong session. Bind the check to the launch's own dispatch (for example: apply it only while the route's current resolution is the launch-dispatch write, by recording the launch_seq with that write and comparing, or by clearing the binding when the route returns to the Master), and add a test that routes again after an identity-changed bounce.

findings.summary: The launch is decided before an asynchronous warm-up and acted on after it, with nothing asked again in between, and overlapping passes can each begin the same queued launch
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Why it broke: _beginLaunch checks the route, _launchRefusal and store.sessions.getActive, then awaits _deps.launchProject, whose first act is `await warmForLaunch(project)` (a CI probe and a checkout probe, each bounded in seconds, over the network); sessions.launchSession runs only after that await. The comment above the getActive check says it is 'asked last, in the same synchronous step as the decision it guards', and docs/operator-bridge.md says the gateway asks again 'before launching'; neither holds across the await. What can change in that window, and what then happens: (a) a hold is placed on the lane: the session is launched anyway (launchSession refuses only a stopped lane), against the ruling that a held lane refuses; the next pass fails the launch 'held' and the session stays up. (b) The Master closes the message, or the bridge is disabled and a pass abandons the launch: the session is still launched, and launches.begin then throws 'was not queued', which is only logged. (c) Someone starts the project by hand: launchSession answers 'Session already active' with no code, so the launch ends 'launch-refused:REFUSED' and the operator is told it failed, where docs step 5 says that session is the one waited for. (d) server.js runs tick on a bare setInterval of 15 s with no guard against a pass still running; advance() serialises per route through _state.inFlight but _advanceLaunches has no equivalent, so when a warm-up outlasts the interval a second pass reads the same row still 'queued' and enters _beginLaunch too. The first pass launches and records 'waiting-ready'; the second gets 'already active' and launches.end() (WHERE settled_at IS NULL) moves that waiting-ready launch to 'failed': a launch that succeeded is recorded and announced as failed. Who does what wrong: the operator is told a launch failed that did not, or a session is started for a message already closed or a lane already held. Remedy: make the decision and the act one synchronous step. Warm first; then, with no await between them, re-read the launch row (still 'queued'), the route (still held), _launchRefusal and getActive, and call sessions.launchSession. Give _advanceLaunches the same one-at-a-time guard advance() has, so a second pass waits or returns while one is in a launch.

findings.summary: A launch whose step throws on every pass never ends, and holds every launch behind it
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. The only deadline a launch has (READY_WAIT_MS) is evaluated inside _awaitLaunch, after _launchRefusal, store.launchSequences.getBySession and _targetWorkspace have all returned, and a queued launch has no deadline at all. If any of those throws on each pass (a locked store, a control or Medusa read that keeps failing, launches.begin refusing as in the test 'a launch that can neither begin nor end is left for the next pass'), the launch stays waiting-ready or queued indefinitely. Because one launch is in flight on the install and the queued loop breaks on a throw, every later consented launch waits behind it. The operator who said yes is sent nothing, the route keeps no failure code, tc bridge read goes on showing 'in flight' or 'waiting its turn', and the only signal is one log.warn per tick with no limit. docs/operator-bridge.md promises ready-timeout after ten minutes, and ruling 6 says no starvation; neither holds on this path. Give the deadline one owner that does not depend on the checks succeeding: in _advanceLaunches, before judging, end any unsettled launch older than a bound (startedAt for waiting-ready, requestedAt plus a queue bound for queued) through _launchFailed with a closed code, and catch a throw from _awaitLaunch there so the age check still runs. Log the repeated failure once per launch rather than every pass. Pin it with a test in which a waiting-ready launch's check throws past the ten minutes.

findings.summary: After a consented launch, the Master can never route that message to the same project again once its session has changed, and is told 'identity-changed' each time
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance (dispatch, the launches.latestFor check). Sequence: launch consented, message sent on, the exchange later fails or the session is replaced, the route returns to awaiting-master; the project is now live under a new session; the Master runs tc bridge route to it (accepted, since liveTarget is true); dispatch has a new request id and no exchange, reads the old dispatched launch, sees a different session and returns the route to the Master as identity-changed. findings.summary: A pin or a reply still suggests a project that is out of reach: two of the suggestion's sources do not pass through the one resolver
findings.recommendation: Scope: class, bounded to lib/bridge-gateway.js#suggestDestination. Only the `@name` branch goes through `bridgeReach.named`. The consequence is the Master being advised to a destination it will be refused, on an opted-out project the operator took out of reach as policy. No test covers it: the opt-out and scope tests assert 'not suggested' for the address branch only. Fix by construction, not per branch: judge every project destination `suggestDestination` is about to return with `bridgeReach.outOfReach` at its one exit, and return no suggestion with a closed reason when it is out of reach; add a test for a pinned conversation and a reply after an opt-out and under an unresolved scope. An operator pin or alias may still be stored for an out-of-reach project (`operatorSetAlias`/`operatorSetPin` use `_destinationFrom`); that is the operator's own write and is not the defect, provided reading it is filtered.

findings.summary: How a project stands is worked out twice, and the two answers can disagree: ask-launch says 'route it' while route says 'ask-launch'
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. Why it broke: 5fca4c02 moved askLaunch onto bridgeReach.liveness (which classifies from ALL active session rows and which of them have a listener) while routeTo, dispatch, _beginLaunch and _awaitLaunch still pick the target through gateway._targetWorkspace / store.sessions.getActive (the NEWEST active row only, and only when it also has a launch-sequence row). In (4) and (5) liveness answers 'live' and _targetWorkspace answers null, so: tc bridge destinations prints 'running'; tc bridge route is refused 409 TARGET_OFFLINE with 'ask the operator whether to launch one with tc bridge ask-launch'; tc bridge ask-launch is refused 409 TARGET_LIVE with 'Route the message with tc bridge route'. Project ids are sequential, so a later project taking that id is the expected case, not a rare one. A Master told 'I meant the nickname' and typing the nickname sends the operator's message to a different project. Over the raw API the string '57' goes through named() and is refused ambiguous, so the two resolvers the design says must be one function disagree here. This is the one way found to write a name that means two things; case, whitespace, leading '@', unicode (the regex is ASCII after lower-casing; only U+212A lower-cases into it, and the key stored is the ASCII one), rename onto an existing name, rename onto a project's name, 'master' in any case, and concurrent writes (the clash is judged and written inside one synchronous transaction) are all closed. findings.summary: Why a name names nothing is worked out twice in bridge-reach, by different rules
findings.recommendation: Scope: class, bounded to lib/bridge-reach.js. The new whyUnnamed() answers 'this name would mean something were its project in reach' from a nickname, a case-insensitive project name, or an id. resolve()'s closing lines answer the same question for the Master's writes with store.projects.getByName(to): exact case, project name only, no nickname. So for a nickname whose project is opted out, the gateway's suggestion says address-out-of-reach and the Master's 'tc bridge route --to <that nickname>' is answered 400 UNKNOWN_DESTINATION ('Name the destination exactly'), and the same split happens for a project name typed in another case. Beneath that, 'does this project answer to this key' (lower-cased name, slug, numeric id) is written out three times, in named(), nicknameClash() and whyUnnamed(), and whyUnnamed's copy leaves the slug out, so an out-of-reach project addressed by slug reads address-unresolved. Make one predicate for 'project answers to key' that all three use, and have resolve() take its out-of-reach reason from whyUnnamed rather than a second lookup; the module's header promises 'one answer, asked by everything that needs it'.

findings.summary: The operator's alias route validates a nickname with its own copy of the shape and reservation rules
findings.recommendation: Scope: class, bounded: search for the pattern [a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}. It is in lib/bridge-api.js twice (the NICKNAME constant behind _nickname(), and inline in operatorSetAlias), in lib/tc-verbs.js, in public/operator-bridge-panel.js, and upper-and-lower in lib/bridge-gateway.js's address pattern. The CLI and browser copies cross a process boundary; the two in bridge-api.js do not. operatorSetAlias does not call _nickname(): it lower-cases without stripping '@', tests its own pattern, and refuses 'master' itself as ALIAS_RESERVED before reaching bridgeReach.nicknameClash. Three consequences. The same condition has two codes by caller (BAD_ALIAS, ALIAS_RESERVED, ALIAS_NOT_FOUND against BAD_NICKNAME, NICKNAME_RESERVED, NICKNAME_NOT_FOUND). NICKNAME_CLASH's 'reserved' and 'exists' entries can never be returned: the operator route is the table's only reader, it handles 'master' first, and it passes the alias as its own replacement so 'exists' cannot arise; the Master's refusals carry a generated 'The nickname was not changed: nickname-collides.' instead of the table's wording. And the display value's .replace(/^@/, '') in operatorSetAlias is unreachable, since a leading '@' has already failed the pattern. A change to what a nickname may look like made in one copy leaves a name the Master can store and the panel's Forget refuses as 'No such nickname', or the gateway never recognises as an address. Have operatorSetAlias go through _nickname() and nicknameClash alone, drop the two unreachable entries or use the table for the Master's answer too, and export the one pattern for lib/tc-verbs.js.

findings.summary: A nickname set refused for where it points leaves no audit row, though the docs say every such refusal does
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. lib/bridge-api.js#setNickname checks the name's shape and resolves 'to' through _reachable() before _nicknameWrite, and returns those refusals directly. Route, pin and launch writes pass the same refusal through _refusedWrite, which audits it. The nickname table in docs/operator-bridge.md answers an unreachable target 'As for any destination, below', and that passage says the refusal is 'on the audit by its code'; CHANGELOG's reach entry says 'A Master write refused for where it points is on the audit by its code'; lib/bridge-store.js#applyNicknameWrite's JSDoc says a nickname change is audited 'applied or refused, like every other Master write'. Resolve the destination inside the change callback and refuse through it, or audit the early refusal as the other writes do.

findings.summary: Nickname audit rows record less than the approved design and the doc say: a refusal has no name, a rename or forget has no target
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance (three sites). (1) lib/bridge-store.js#applyNicknameWrite: refused() records the outcome with detail null, so a nickname-exists, nickname-collides, nickname-not-found or instruction-used row names the route and the code but not the nickname that was tried. (2) lib/bridge-api.js#renameNickname records {nickname, was} and #forgetNickname records {was}: neither holds what the nickname pointed at. (3) #operatorRemoveAlias records {alias, user} only. The decision plan's bounded design, part 3, says 'The audit row holds the nickname before and after, the target project id and the route ids', and docs/operator-bridge.md says 'the audit records the nickname, the target and the message's route id'. That holds for set and not for rename or forget. A forget deletes the row, so what the name meant is then only in the earlier nickname-set row, which audit compaction may remove once that route is closed and old. Applied writes are otherwise fully attributable: actor, proof, Master generation, the operator message's route id, and for the operator the signed-in user. Rated note because the gap changes what can be reconstructed, not what anyone does. If it is closed, read the row inside the change callback and add the destination to the rename and forget detail, and pass the attempted name into refused(). Otherwise narrow the doc sentence to set.

observations.summary: On the reply path nothing requires the @master message to be routed to the Master, before or after the change
observations.recommendation: Scope: instance. lib/bridge-store.js applyNicknameWrite, reply branch: the question's route must carry the recorded @master marker, the reply must be the adoptable answer to a clarify question, and the route must not have authorised a change already. It does not check where that route was or will be routed, and it cannot at write time, because a question can only be asked while the message is still held. After the change the Master is free to route the original to a project or close it; only its standing instructions say to route it to itself. No message not written to @master gains authority this way. The Architect's sentence says 'explicitly addressed to @master and routed by Master to itself', and the ADR's new paragraph reads 'a reply authorises a change only when its question was about such a message', where 'such' includes 'the Master routed to itself'. If the Architect means addressed-to-@master, the code matches and no edit is wanted. If the ruling means the original must also end up with the Master, that is a requirement the code does not enforce, and closing it means the nickname write routing the original to the Master in the same transaction. This is a question for the Architect, not a commit. ACCEPT is the default once the reading is confirmed.

observations.summary: The forged-row assertion passes with or without the new actor = 'gateway' clause, so the clause is not pinned
observations.recommendation: Scope: instance. test/api-bridge-gateway.test.js appends a master-actor 'suggest' row with reserved: true to the route toProject, which already carries the gateway's own suggest row (the test asserts suggestion(toProject).by === 'alias' two lines earlier). audit.addressedToMaster orders by audit_seq and takes the first row; audit_seq is INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT (lib/bridge-schema.js line 509), so the forged row always sorts after the gateway's, whose detail has no 'reserved' key. The query returns false and the write is refused NOT_AN_INSTRUCTION under the old query and the new one alike. The 'at' of 2000-01-01 on the forged row has no effect, because nothing orders by 'at'. Deleting the clause from lib/bridge-store.js line 361 would leave this test green, so the commit message's 'Pinned with a row of the same kind under another writer' does not hold. The production clause itself is correct and matches the gateway writer (lib/bridge-gateway.js _step defaults actor to 'gateway'; _advance line 526 passes no override), and no other writer of op 'suggest' exists in lib/, so nothing in the tree behaves wrongly. I did not rate it blocking for that reason: the state the clause guards cannot be produced by production code. A discriminating test needs a route whose only applied suggest row is the other writer's. bridge_audit.route_id has no foreign key, so a store-level test can append a master-actor suggest row with reserved: true under a fresh route id and assert addressedToMaster is false, then append a gateway-actor one and assert true. ACCEPT is the default; fixing it costs a round, so it rides a commit already planned if there is one.

observations.summary: The reply-path nickname write is one transaction and matches the Master's own route write; prior observation O-3 is answered
observations.recommendation: Scope: none. No edit is wanted. Read lib/bridge-store.js applyNicknameWrite (lines 1971-2044) against transaction() (line 27), questions.adoptVerdict and settleOnReply (lines 2143-2196), _applyRouteWrite (lines 2476-2573) and lib/bridge-api.js routeTo (lines 605-643). Every effect (alias write inside change(), the route UPDATE, the question settle, the reply route close, the route audit row, _noLongerHeld, the applied audit row) runs inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and any throw rolls all of it back. Every refusal returns before change() writes or, for a refused change, before the route UPDATE; the three change callbacks in bridge-api.js write only as their last step, so a refusal commits its own audit row and nothing else. The not-awaiting-master check sits after adoptVerdict and usedUp and before change(), so it consumes nothing. The hand-written UPDATE sets the same columns routeTo sets for a master destination (state accepted, resolved_by master, destination_kind master, destination_project_id NULL, resolved_generation, failure_code NULL, version + 1, updated_at) and is fenced on version and state. It skips no guard routeTo applies on the same path: routeTo sets no withdraw, and _applyRouteWrite skips the in-flight question check when the write adopts (leavingHeld && !decision.adopt), while adoptVerdict's own outbound.inFlight check on the reply runs on both paths. The order settle-then-_noLongerHeld is the same as _applyRouteWrite's, so the adopted question is not cancelled and queued launches are abandoned. The Master generation is proven the way it is for every Master write: PRINCIPALS.master accepts only the active generation's credential (bridge-principal.js verify, findActive) and revokes on a Master that is not live, with no await between that proof and the synchronous transaction.

observations.summary: After a failed or interrupted gateway.advance, a replay tells the Master to answer a message that is not yet answerable
observations.recommendation: Scope: instance (lib/bridge-api.js _nicknameWrite lines 1499-1503 with lib/tc-verbs.js line 1675). The decision is durable at commit: the route is accepted with destination master, and the gateway pass sweeps accepted routes (lib/bridge-gateway.js line 1454), so nothing is lost if advance throws or the process stops. In that window the first call fails as a server error after the change committed, and a retry with the same request id is a replay that does not advance, so it reports instruction.state accepted while the CLI prints 'is now yours ... do not route it, answer it'. An answer before the next pass (15 seconds) would be refused. The Master's own route write has the same gap, as built. ACCEPT is the default; if it is ever changed, advancing on a replay too would close it.

observations.summary: Advancing on a replay is safe, and the prior observation O-2 is answered
observations.recommendation: Scope: none. No edit is wanted. Read lib/bridge-api.js _nicknameWrite (lines 1484-1512) against lib/bridge-gateway.js advance/_advance (501-536), _needsMaster (544-548), dispatch (610-613), _summonMaster (1143-1167), _tellMaster (1177-1204) and the periodic pass (1454-1459). The replay now makes the same advance(routeId) call the 15-second pass makes for every open route, so it adds no behaviour the pass does not already perform. By state: accepted with destination master takes one version-fenced step to routed; routed to the Master only reaches _tellMaster, which is told once per routeId:version; an answered or closed route matches neither branch of _advance and is untouched; a route since re-routed to a project is sent under the per-attempt request id, which finds the existing exchange and does not send twice; a route that no longer exists returns null and the answer carries instruction: null. Calls for one route are serialised through _state.inFlight. The one repeat is a second system notice to the Master after a server restart, because mastersTold is in memory; the pass does the same.
